parsed.explanation: The combined regime is protective and visitor-friendly on paper and largely in practice: no trans-specific criminal offence, hate speech and anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, self-declaration legal recognition, a functioning hate-crime framework with demonstrated enforcement (30-year sentence for the Pride shooter), and top-level political condemnation of anti-trans hate. No border, facility, custody, or care restriction on visitors is documented. The main negatives are societal-incident-level: an isolated mass shooting (perpetrated by an ideological extremist, firmly punished, now assessed declining by the security service), rising reported hate crime with a falling clearance rate, and low victim trust in police (tier 3 friction with partial recourse). For minors travelling with guardians, no visitor-facing restriction is documented; only resident-facing care pathways are narrow. This sits in the Low Risk band, just below the strongest anchors because of the documented enforcement-trust gap and residual ideological hostility.

entry_documents.exposure: Not documented. No border or document-screening friction for trans visitors appears anywhere in the record.
entry_documents.protection: Self-declaration legal recognition and foreign-citizen provisions signal an accepting institutional document culture.
entry_documents.interaction: No interaction between documents and investigation or refusal documented.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Not documented for visitors; no trans-specific detention or custody placement exposure recorded.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Hate-crime framework with offender sentencing (30-year maximum) shows criminal justice working against, not for, anti-trans violence.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Clearance-rate fall (52%→45%) and 8% reporting rate mean crimes may go unremedied, but no custody exposure follows.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Not documented. No bathroom, ward, or facility rule reaches visitors in the record.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Anti-discrimination law since 2013 covers goods and services including gender expression.

care_services.exposure: Visitors' emergency/ordinary care not documented as restricted; the narrow quarter-of-referrals bottleneck and licence revocation case concern residents' transition care, not traveller-facing denial.
care_services.protection: 2020 guideline forbids denial and frames care on informed consent; reimbursement infrastructure exists.
care_services.interaction: Uncertain whether a trans visitor needing refills could navigate the specialist channel — an open question, not a documented exposure.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Organised ideological anti-trans hostility (far-right, gender-critical networks), online threats, tabloid incitement; 2022 Pride shooting; knife attack.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Prime ministerial condemnation, penal-code hate speech coverage, strict sentencing, security service reporting declining threats aimed mostly at spreading fear.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Extremist hostility is concentrated and monitored rather than street-level and diffuse.

minors_guardians.exposure: Not documented for visiting minors; no entry, facility or restriction touches a trans minor travelling with a guardian.
minors_guardians.protection: LGR route allows joint parental application ages 6–16; supportive counselling framework exists.
minors_guardians.interaction: Only resident-facing youth-care debates (2023 board finding) are turbulent; nothing operative against visitors.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: LGBT people report hate comments/threats at 2–4× general rate; capital bias-crime counts show LGBT second-largest category; one shooting, one knife attack — incident-level, not a campaign.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Offenders prosecuted (30 years), hate-crime framework operative, dedicated reporting group, security service threat decline.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Only 8% of victims report; dismissive treatment and falling clearance blunt practical recourse.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Undercounted hate crime with weak trust in police is the main remedy gap; border/facility screening practices are unanswered questions, not exposures.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Civil society infrastructure, helplines, hate-crime reporting channels, and working courts documented.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Reporting barriers reduce effective recourse but do not create custody or punishment risk for the victim.

anchor_checks.comparison: Very close: both have explicit GI anti-discrimination law, functioning oversight, one imperfect rural/individual incident, and broad tolerance. This jurisdiction's documented shooting, lower police trust (8% reporting), and falling clearance rate sit slightly below that anchor's cleaner remedy record, but its stricter sentencing of the perpetrator compensates.

Below 0.95-D, whose hospitality remedies and courteous climate show no violent incidents at all. Here an actual mass shooting, knife attack, and quantified hate-crime rise exist, so the jurisdiction cannot reach that tier despite comparable legal machinery.

Above 0.75-D, where late-night assaults recur and officer failure-to-act is a live pattern. Here violence is rarer, ideologically concentrated, the worst offender received the maximum sentence, and the security service reports threats declining; only reporting-trust friction is comparable.

parsed.synthesis: The combined operative regime for a trans visitor is one of embedded legal protection with an imperfect enforcement tail. Exposures are societal and incident-based (extremist violence, online intimidation, a hostile press minority) rather than state-imposed or universal: no rule touches borders, documents, facilities, custody, or care access for visitors. Protections are real and operative — hate-speech liability since 2020, service anti-discrimination since 2013, maximum sentence actually imposed on a shooter, and top-level state solidarity. The friction point is recourse quality: falling clearance and low reporting trust mean an outed visitor may receive dismissive police handling after a hate incident. That caps the score in the upper 0.8s rather than the 0.95 tier; nothing in the dossier supports material physical danger beyond a background level common to the society, and travelling with a minor adds no documented exposure.
